transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Jared Mills (Acme Head of ML), Sofia Chen (Acme Platform Eng), Ravi Patel (Acme SRE)

Summary (auto): align on benchmark methodology, share artifacts, run controlled tests, follow-up.

[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone thanks for joining today, um this is Alex from Redwood, and with me is Priya our SE. we're hoping to run through a repeatable benchmark methodology so we can do apples to apples comparisons between hosted, dedicated and your on-prem setup.
[00:12] Jared Mills: yeah thanks Alex, we really want to understand tail latency under load and also how kv cache priming impacts costs. we've seen big swings in our own tiny tests.
[00:22] Priya Desai: cool, quick agenda: prompt set design, load generator config, cache priming and warmup, batching params, quantization profiles, and VPC/on-prem infra considerations. then next steps.
[00:38] Sofia Chen: sounds good. my main constraints are network egress limits for the VPC, and we need to prove data never leaves our VPC for the on-prem run, so that will affect how we run the load generator.
[00:49] Ravi Patel: and from SRE, our success criteria are p95 < 200ms for short completion prompts and predictable throughput at at least 200 req/s for long chat-like prompts.
[01:05] Alex Kim: good, that's helpful. couple quick definitions so we're aligned: when we say p95 we're talking about end-to-end server-side latency excluding client-side network variance, right?
[01:14] Jared Mills: yep, server-side only. we can instrument tcp for client network if needed but for apples-to-apples we want server-side.
[01:22] Priya Desai: perfect. point one: prompt sets. we recommend a three-tier prompt set: micro (<=32 tokens), standard (~64-256 tokens), and long/streaming (>512 tokens). include distribution matching production percentiles. for acme retail, like checkout bot messages are micro/standard, product descriptions are long.
[01:44] Sofia Chen: question: should we include system messages and tool calls in the prompts? our prod traffic has a lot of tool calls which add tokens to the request.
[01:52] Priya Desai: yes include representative system messages and any tool call overhead because kv cache hit rates and batch formation are affected. also note that tool calls often change the token distribution during generation which affects kv cache size.
[02:06] Alex Kim: also a note that in some transcriptions our product name gets munged, sorry Redwood, we keep seeing 'red wood' in earlier notes haha.
[02:13] (laughter)
[02:20] [02:20] Jared Mills: about load generation — we should use a closed-loop load generator that replays arrival patterns, not just constant qps, to capture realistic latency spikes.
[02:33] Priya Desai: we typically recommend a synthetic harness we fork from our internal benchmark repo: it supports poisson arrivals, burst windows, configurable think times, and measures p50/p95/p99 and token throughput. we'll share the repo link.
[02:47] Alex Kim: note: important to run with cold-starts and hot-warm comparisons. for KV cache priming, run three phases: cold (no cache), warm (primed with representative prefixes), and steady-state (continuous traffic with cache eviction simulation).
[03:05] Ravi Patel: can you explain priming? in our small tests priming seemed to reduce latency by, like, 30-40% on average for some prompts.
[03:13] Priya Desai: sure. priming means pre-loading the KV cache with prefixes that match your prompt set so when requests hit the model, key-value lookups are cache hits rather than re-computes. this is very beneficial for high-reuse prompt patterns. but be mindful of cache capacity and eviction.
[03:29] Jared Mills: and is the cache size per model shard or per instance?
[03:33] Priya Desai: depends on runtime; in Redwood Dedicated we shard the KV cache across GPU workers, and for private they can be per-node or shared depending on deployment. important for apples-to-apples: configure cache sizes equivalently across envs, or normalize metrics by cache hit-rate.
[03:49] [03:49] Sofia Chen: got it. next: batching. we saw in our pilot that increasing max batch size improved throughput but increased p95. what's your recommended approach for balancing?
[03:59] Priya Desai: classic tradeoff. for latency-sensitive use-cases you want smaller max batch and tight batching windows; for throughput you increase batch size and allow slightly higher latency. we'd recommend running a sweep: vary max_batch_size and max_latency_ms for the batching window, record throughput vs p95, and plot pareto fronts.
[04:18] Alex Kim: also test continuous batching vs opportunistic batching. opportunistic helps when you have bursty arrivals because it won't always wait to fill large batches. include both in the benchmark matrix.
[04:29] [04:29] Ravi Patel: any gotchas for quantization? our infra team is worried about quality regressions after int8 quantization even if latency improves.
[04:37] Priya Desai: totally. quantization gives great latency/cost wins but you must quantify quality using the same prompt set and evaluation metrics. run A/B quality tests: compute embedding similarity, token-level accuracy for known outputs, and run human-review on ambiguous cases. also test end-to-end latency; quantization can change kernel dispatch patterns which impact tail latency sometimes.
transcript_continued:
[04:58] Jared Mills: do we need to normalize GPU types across environments? our private data center has A100s while Redwood hosted uses A800s in some regions.
[05:08] Priya Desai: yes, normalize by hardware or report per-GPU metrics. for apples-to-apples, document GPU model, driver versions, CUDA/cuDNN, and throughput per GPU. if you can't match hardware, report performance per TFLOP or per-GPU-second and call out the differences.
[05:25] Alex Kim: also include compilation/kernels: different runtimes choose different kernels for attention that can change latency; capture runtime flags and library versions.
[05:33] [05:33] Sofia Chen: network considerations for VPC/on-prem: do you recommend colocating load generator inside the same VPC vs outside?
[05:42] Priya Desai: colocate the load generator to remove internet variance when measuring server-side processing. for on-prem we prefer running the harness inside the customer's network so egress is zero and you can measure internal fabric latency. capture NIC stats and any network shaping.
[05:58] Jared Mills: what about metrics collection — what should we instrument?
[06:02] Alex Kim: server-side request/response timestamps, GPU utilization, memory/kv cache hit rates, batch sizes per-second, kernel latencies, and process-level GC or python overhead. collect system metrics at high frequency to align with request traces.
[06:17] Ravi Patel: you mentioned kernel latencies — we saw spikes tied to kernel re-compilation when sequence lengths jumped. how do we avoid that?
[06:25] Priya Desai: pre-compile the common shapes where possible and warm up with a representative mix of sequence lengths. also record compilation events in the runtime logs so you can exclude them or flag them in analysis.
[06:38] [06:38] Jared Mills: one organizational question — how do we make sure test results are reproducible? we've had drift between runs.
[06:46] Alex Kim: lock the software stack: container images with exact runtime versions, pinned drivers, fixed seeds for stochastic components, and capture random seeds used. persist the input corpus and the harness config in git. also provide the raw traces and a notebook that reproduces the analysis so others can validate.
[07:04] Sofia Chen: about security/compliance: we need to ensure logs with token-level outputs aren't stored outside the VPC. how do you handle that in Redwood Private?
[07:13] Priya Desai: in Private we support customer-managed logging and integrations with customer KMS. for bench runs you can disable logging of raw tokens, or redact data before sending metrics. we also support audit logs that don't contain sensitive payloads.
[07:26] [07:26] Ravi Patel: any specific SOC2/ISO artifacts we should ask for during the pilot?
[07:31] Alex Kim: we'll share the SOC2 Type II report and ISO certs, plus a security whitepaper. we'll also provide an architecture diagram for the private deployment showing KMS boundaries.
[07:42] Priya Desai: another practical note: measure warmup behavior over longer windows. some caches achieve better hit rates over hours, not minutes, depending on reuse patterns; make sure your steady-state window is long enough to be meaningful.
[07:56] Jared Mills: let's talk about measurement slices — how granular should we be? per-route, per-model-version?
[08:03] Priya Desai: per-route and per-model-version is ideal. include labels for prompt-type, customer route, and model variant. that way you can detect regressions when you change quantization or kernel flags.
[08:15] [08:15] Sofia Chen: our legal team also wants to track data residency. if we run hosted benchmarks in region 'eu-west-1' versus our on-prem EU DC, we need to show where data resided.
[08:26] Alex Kim: fair. include region metadata and storage location in the benchmark artifact. for on-prem runs note the subnet/cluster name.
[08:36] [08:36] Jared Mills: fine. let's walk through an example benchmark matrix quickly: dimension lines could be model_variant x quantization x batch_config x load_pattern x cache_state. anyone else?
[08:49] Priya Desai: yep and add environment (hosted/dedicated/private) as a top-level axis. then run combinations but prioritize plausible real-world combos to limit total runs.
[08:58] Alex Kim: and for analysis we'll produce latency vs throughput curves, and a quality regression matrix comparing baseline to quantized/optimized runs. include cost per 1M tokens estimate.
[09:10] [09:10] Ravi Patel: cost estimates are important for execs. show both token cost and infra amortized cost for on-prem.
[09:17] Priya Desai: we can help with a template spreadsheet that computes cost per token and per request given GPU hours and utilization.
[09:24] [09:24] Jared Mills: okay, operationally who owns running these tests on our side vs Redwood?
[09:29] Alex Kim: Redwood will share the harness and run a hosted baseline. Acme will run the private/on-prem harness and share traces; Redwood can assist with running dedicated tests if you provide access to the Dedicated pool or accept our managed run.
[09:42] Sofia Chen: about the VPC private deployment, is there a lightweight on-prem bundle or do we need full infra?
[09:49] Priya Desai: we have a slim installer for evaluation that runs in a customer VPC with minimal components, but for production we recommend the full stack. the eval bundle can run with a single machine for small workloads; for realistic benching you should size to at least 2-4 GPU nodes.
[10:03] [10:03] Jared Mills: anything else on observability? we want traces that map from API request through batching and kernel timings.
[10:11] Alex Kim: instrument the runtime to emit trace ids and batch ids; include a sampling of full request payloads (redacted) to correlate. we'll provide log parsing scripts to join traces with GPU metrics.
[10:22] Priya Desai: last segment — pitfalls to watch for: misaligned prompt distributions, unpinned stacks, measuring client network vs server latency, not priming caches, and comparing different GPU generations without normalization.
[10:34] Ravi Patel: noted. can you share the exact steps you'll email over so we don't miss anything?
[10:39] Alex Kim: yep, will send a checklist: repo link, prompt set template, harness config, metrics to collect, and example analysis notebook.
[10:47] [10:47] Jared Mills: great. quick recap of next steps?
[10:50] Alex Kim: recap: (1) Alex to send benchmark repo and prompt templates by 2025-03-05; (2) Acme to provide production traffic profile and spin up VPC test env by 2025-03-10; (3) Run initial runs and share traces by 2025-03-12; (4) follow-up meeting week of 2025-03-17 to review results.
[11:10] Sofia Chen: that schedule works for our team.
[11:14] Priya Desai: cool, thanks everyone — we'll be available for support while you run the harness.
[11:19] Jared Mills: thanks all, appreciate it.
[11:22] (call ends)
